title: TC0-09893
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): For reasons that follow, I dismiss the appeal and confirm the RPD's determination that the Appellant is not a Convention1 refugee or a person in need of protection because she has a viable IFA in Nigeria.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: The Appellant, XXXX XXXX XXXX, a citizen of Nigeria, is appealing the rejection of her refugee claim by the Refugee Protection Division (RPD). The Appellant alleges that she faces a serious possibility of persecution or a risk to life or cruel and unusual treatment or punishment in Nigeria at the hands of her husband's family who accuses her of witchcraft.

The determinative issue in this appeal is internal flight alternative (IFA). For reasons that follow, I dismiss the appeal and confirm the RPD's determination that the Appellant is not a Convention1 refugee or a person in need of protection because she has a viable IFA in Nigeria.

The Appellant married her husband, a Canadian citizen, on XXXX XXXX, 2015. After the marriage, she moved into his family home in Ile-Ife where she took care of her mother-in-law. She started having issues with her husband's family when they accused her of not taking proper care of her mother-in-law. In XXXX 2016, her sister-in-law came to visit with her son. Subsequently, the young boy fell ill and died. The Appellant's in-laws blamed her for causing the boy's illness and death. The Appellant's brother-in-law also lost his job during this time. Again, her husband's family blamed her for their misfortune.

The Appellant's in-laws accused her of being a witch and consulted an oracle priest who instructed them to bring the Appellant for rituals at a shrine. The Appellant refused because, as a Christian, these rituals were against her religious beliefs. On XXXX XXXX, 2016 the Appellant overheard some people chanting that they "will sacrificed her for {Sango} god of thunder and {Ogun} god of iron."2 The Appellant fled to her friend XXXX house for the night before fleeing to Ibadan. After staying with her cousin in Ibadan for a week, she continued on to Lagos to stay with her childhood friend. After her friend's husband complained, the Appellant left Lagos and travelled to the United States (US). She remained there for just over a year before crossing into Canada and claiming refugee status.

Due to a lack of evidence corroborating the Appellant's allegations and an unsatisfactory explanation for not obtaining such documents, the RPD made a negative credibility finding. Given the Appellant was represented by competent Counsel and had sufficient time before the hearing, the RPD found that it was reasonable to expect, in the circumstances, that some documentation could have reasonably been obtained to support the Appellant's central allegations. The RPD drew a negative credibility inference because it doubted the truthfulness of the Appellant's allegations.

The Appellant travelled to the US and remained there for just over a year before coming to Canada and making a refugee claim. The Appellant did not try to claim asylum in the US, however she made two applications for Canadian visitor visas while living there; both were rejected. Despite acknowledging that the Appellant's intention was to join her husband in Canada, the RPD found that her failure to make a refugee claim in the US raised serious doubt as to the Appellant's subjective fear.

The RPD also made an alternative finding, identifying Lagos, Abuja, and Port Harcourt as viable IFAs in Nigeria. The RPD focused on the size of these cities, the distance from where the Appellant was living with her in-laws, the substantial Christian population, and the fact that her husband testified he would provide her financial support in Nigeria, to find that the Appellant was not a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. The RPD also noted that the Appellant was able to stay in Ibadan and Lagos for approximately five weeks before leaving Nigeria without incident or pursuit from the agents of persecution.

Furthermore, the RPD found that the Appellant failed to demonstrate how the proposed IFAs were objectively unreasonable. The RPD canvassed the Appellant's psychological report and found that the Appellant failed to establish that her mental health concerns made relocating to the IFAs unduly harsh. The RPD cited the Appellant's business experience, her education, her competence to travel alone, lack of dependents, and the financial support from her husband to find that resettlement in one of the proposed IFAs would not be objectively unreasonable. Appellant's arguments

I will only deal with the Appellant's arguments relevant to the determinative issue of IFA. The Appellant argues that the RPD breached procedural fairness by failing to apply the Chairperson's Guideline 4 - Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-Related Persecution3 (Gender Guidelines) in its analysis of the claim and erred in not considering the Appellant's personal circumstances during the IFA analysis. Role of the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD)

The Federal Court of Appeal in Huruglica4 held that I must review RPD decisions on a correctness standard where questions of law, fact, and mixed fact and law raise no issue of the credibility of oral evidence. I have done an independent assessment of all the evidence before me and reviewed the RPD decision on a standard of correctness. ANALYSIS The RPD did not breach procedural fairness

I find that the RPD did not commit a breach of procedural fairness. According to the Policy on the use of Chairperson's Guidelines, although not legally binding, Guidelines are "intended to be considered by members of the tribunal in appropriate cases"5 unless compelling or exceptional reasons exist to depart from them. Failure to expressly mention the Guidelines does not vitiate a decision,6 however, the reasons for the decision should demonstrate findings were made considering the factors set out in the Guidelines. The Guidelines are not intended to serve as a cure for all the deficiencies in the evidence; the question is whether the RPD was responsive to the factors which may influence testimony.7

On appeal, the Appellant alleges that the RPD failed to adequately consider the Gender Guidelines. The Appellant argues the RPD failed to be sensitive to her gender, the social, cultural, economic, and religious norms of her community, and "to the factors which may influence the testimony of women who have been victims of persecution."8 Furthermore, the Appellant argues the RPD failed to consider her state of mind and psychological make-up when evaluating her evidence. The Appellant has failed to specifically explain in what way the RPD failed to apply the Gender Guidelines or in which way the Gender Guidelines should have been applied.

I disagree with the Appellant's vague arguments and conclude that the RPD adequately applied the Gender Guidelines in its analysis. The RPD explicitly acknowledges the Gender Guidelines at paragraph 32 of its decision. It also substantively applied the Gender Guidelines in the second prong of its IFA analysis. The RPD acknowledged the Appellant's arguments about why the proposed IFAs were objectively unreasonable-she suffered from anxiety, abandoned her trading equipment for her self-employed business, that she would have difficulty obtaining accommodation, and men might take advantage of her as a single woman. The RPD also acknowledged the unique challenges for single women relocating in Nigeria. Furthermore, the RPD considered the psychological report submitted by the Appellant, comprising a morning interview based on the Appellant's self-reported information. In any event, I have also conducted an independent assessment of all the evidence and have applied the Gender Guidelines below. Credibility

Sworn testimony is presumed to be true unless there are reasons to doubt its truthfulness.9 Despite my credibility concerns, I have identified the determinative issue as IFA, therefore, I accept the Appellant's allegations regarding her in-laws-the agents of persecution. Given I am accepting the Appellant's allegations as true, I will not deal with her arguments that the RPD erred with respect to its negative credibility findings based on a lack of corroborative documents or subjective fear. Internal Flight Alternative

There are two prongs to the IFA analysis. The first deals with whether the Appellant faces a serious possibility that she would be persecuted or subjected personally to a risk to life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment in the proposed IFA. The second prong of the test asks whether, in all the circumstances, including those particular to the Appellant, conditions in the proposed IFA are such that it would be objectively unreasonable for her to seek refuge there.10 The standard is a very high threshold and requires that the Appellant demonstrates the presence of adverse conditions which would jeopardize her life and safety.11 If the Appellant can establish either prong of the test on a balance of probabilities, then the proposed IFA is not viable. The Appellant does not face a serious possibility of persecution in Lagos or Abuja

The Appellant argues that she faces persecution in Nigeria because her in-laws have shown the willingness, determination, and resources to pursue her in any part of Nigeria. I completely disagree; the Appellant has failed to provide any evidence that her husband's family have either the desire or the means to pursue her in the Lagos or Abuja. Although the Appellant's neighbour told her that her in-laws had called the police, there is no evidence that the police are interested in her or have taken any steps to pursue her. According to the Appellant's basis of claim narrative, she even considered reporting the incident to the police, but thought the police would not do anything to help.

I would like to note that the Appellant stayed with her cousin in Ibadan for approximately one week. The Appellant subsequently went to stay with a childhood friend in Lagos for some weeks before leaving for the US. According to her basis of claim narrative, the Appellant left her childhood friend's home in Lagos when her friend's husband began to complain. The Appellant provided no testimony or documentary evidence of being sought out by the alleged agents of persecution in Ibadan or Lagos. When asked why she could not move to Lagos, or Abuja, or Port Harcourt, the Appellant testified that she no longer had her catering equipment, people do not give accommodation to single women, and she feared sexual harassment from landlords. She did not mention anything about the alleged agents of persecution. I find that the Appellant has failed to establish that the alleged agents of persecution have the motivation or means to find her in the proposed IFAs. It is not objectively unreasonable for the Appellant to relocate to Lagos or Abuja

I find that it would not be objectively unreasonable or unduly harsh for the Appellant to relocate to Lagos or Abuja. I disagree with the Appellant's argument that the RPD erred in failing to consider the Appellant's age, gender, level of education, ethnicity, religion, financial circumstances, ability to make a livelihood, accommodation, and support network in the proposed IFAs. Furthermore, I agree with the RPD's assessment of the Appellant's personal circumstances during the second prong of its IFA analysis. In its decision, the RPD noted that the proposed IFAs have a substantial Christian population; roughly 40% of Nigerians are Christian.12 Furthermore, the RPD recognized that the proposed IFAs have large multi-ethnic and multi-cultural populations. Finally, the Appellant speaks English and Yoruba-the dominant ethnic group in Lagos13-and should not encounter any language or cultural barriers in relocating there.

The Appellant argues that the RPD failed to consider that she does not have a job or employment in the proposed IFAs. This is incorrect. While the RPD acknowledged that finding employment can be difficult, it also acknowledged that the Appellant has 12 years worth of formal education, significantly higher than the average Nigerian,14 was self-employed and ran a catering business, and is competent to travel on her own. The Appellant also testified that her husband financially supported her while she was in Nigeria. At the RPD hearing, he testified that he is a safety officer in a nuclear plant and a physiotherapist. He also testified that he would continue to financially support her if she returned to Nigeria. Having a husband who will financially support her places the Appellant in a better position then many other single women in Nigeria. I agree with the RPD's analysis and find that the combination of the Appellant's education, business know-how, competence in navigating travel, and financial support from her husband will help facilitate her resettlement in one of the proposed IFA locations.

The Appellant argues that it is difficult for women to find accommodation in those cities without a male counterpart, it is difficult to find employment, and since the Appellant's husband is in Canada, she may be subjected to sexual harassment. I would note that the Appellant has established a business before; her knowledge and experience will be an asset in seeking employment or establishing another business. Furthermore, the objective documentary evidence states that women living in urban areas are 67% more likely to be employed and the employment rate of women generally increased with their level of education.15 Finally, the Appellant has failed to establish how potential sexual harassment rises to the level of persecution or to the level of jeopardizing her life and safety in the proposed IFAs.

The Appellant also argues that the documentary evidence establishes that state and local government sometimes discriminate against non-indigenes respecting accommodation and employment opportunities. The objective documentary evidence also states that these discriminatory practices are not as prevalent in larger centers like Lagos and Abuja.16 The Appellant also submitted an article "Why single Nigerian women battle to rent homes" which highlights how landlords discriminate against single women by insisting to speak with a male partner before letting, and usually prefer renting to men because they have more money.17 According to the NDP, women-headed households who have sufficient funds to cover the cost of rent are more likely to be able to access accommodation.18 I fully acknowledge the challenges that women face finding accommodation due to antiquated patriarchal social views. Having said that, both women at the center of the article were able to secure accommodation after five to six months, one with the help of her then-boyfriend, and the other by using a letting agency.19 There is nothing preventing the Appellant from also accessing a letting agency to help her secure accommodation.

Finally, the Appellant states that the RPD erred in not considering the Appellant's trauma as outlined in the psychological report and its effect on her ability to relocate to the intended IFA locations where she "has no job, no housing, and no support whatsoever."20 It is simply not true that the Appellant has no support whatsoever; the Appellant has significant support from her spouse. Furthermore, after reviewing the psychological report, I agree with the RPD's assessment. I would note that this report was conducted during a morning interview and that most of the information within the document is self-reported by the Appellant. The report describes the Appellant's anxiety and stress regarding the outcome of her refugee claim; something that many refugees experience. Furthermore, the report acknowledges that the Appellant receives emotional support from her husband and a friend in Nigeria whom she misses. The RPD also noted that it had been almost a year and half since the psychological interview and the Appellant had not submitted any evidence of engaging in continued therapy as recommended by the psychologist. I would also note that no such evidence has been provided on appeal. I find that the Appellant has failed to establish that her mental health concerns rise to the level of rendering the proposed IFAs objectively unreasonable or unduly harsh.

While I have no doubt that it is difficult to secure employment and accommodation in Nigeria, I find that the Appellant is well-positioned to accomplish this. She has significant education, has experience running her own catering business, speaks English and Yoruba, is Christian, and has a husband willing to financially support her while in Nigeria. I find that the Appellant has failed to demonstrate, on a balance of probabilities, considering her personal circumstances, that the conditions in the proposed IFAs are so dire as to render it objectively unreasonable or unduly harsh to relocate to Lagos or Abuja.

I dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection because she has a viable IFA in Lagos or Abuja.
